reason: The chamber-shaped heart muscle appears designed to surround the heart chambers and produce a squeeze.
expectation: The muscle will attach to the chambers so they can contract.

effect: The muscular chambers squeeze fluid toward both openings, so valves appear necessary to direct the flow.
reaction: The arrows make the need for valves clear.
reason: The valve picture shows cusps closing against reverse flow, which should help the squeeze drive blood forward.
expectation: The valves will guide fluid forward and prevent backward flow during a squeeze.

effect: The valves direct flow during squeezing and refill; the heart still needs a way to coordinate repeated squeezes.
reaction: The paired panels make the valves’ roles clear.
reason: The pacemaker cells show a spreading electrical wave, suggesting they can coordinate repeated contractions.
expectation: The pacemaker cells will help the heart squeeze repeatedly in a coordinated way.

effect: The pacemaker completes the repeatedly beating pump; I still need blood and a returning vessel route.
reaction: The distinction between starting the beat and nerves adjusting it is useful.
reason: Hemoglobin has oxygen-binding sites, and the flexible red-cell envelopes appear designed to contain it.
expectation: The envelopes and hemoglobin will form oxygen-carrying red cells.

effect: The red cells carry hemoglobin and make ATP from sugar without mitochondria. They need to join the plasma to form blood.
reaction: The contrast with the muscle cells is interesting.
reason: Plasma is the fluid component available to carry the red blood cells.
expectation: The red blood cells and plasma will form blood.

effect: The red cells and plasma formed oxygen-carrying blood, with sugar dissolved in the plasma. I still need a returning vessel route for the pump and blood.
reaction: The inset clarifies that other blood components are included.
reason: Capillary networks appear to connect the branching arteries and veins into a route through tissues.
expectation: The capillaries will connect the arteries and veins into a returning vessel route.

effect: The capillaries connected the arteries and veins, leaving slots for the pump and transport medium.
reaction: The empty slots make the remaining assembly clear.
reason: The beating heart fits the circuit’s pump slot.
expectation: The heart will connect to the vessel circuit as its pump.

effect: The beating heart is connected to the vessel circuit; the transport medium slot remains to be filled.
reaction: The heart-to-vessel inset makes the pump connection clear.
reason: Oxygen-carrying blood fits the circuit's transport medium slot.
expectation: The blood will fill the circuit and circulate through the connected vessels.

effect: The blood completed the circuit. The result shows exchange at capillaries and blood returning to circulate again.
reaction: The distinction between materials crossing the capillary wall and red cells staying inside is useful.

mostWorthwhile.text: Adding the valves was most worthwhile: the squeeze and refill panels explain how they direct flow through the heart.

leastWorthwhile.text: Fitting the heart into the circuit was straightforward, but its inset added less explanation than the earlier heart-building results.

surprise.text: The red blood cells can make ATP from sugar despite having no mitochondria, unlike the muscle cells described earlier.

arbitrary.text: No action felt particularly arbitrary. The pictures and empty slots gave the combinations a clear purpose.

continue.text: I would continue to see how the circulation connects with other body systems. The tissue-exchange picture raises a useful question about how blood gets replenished with oxygen and nutrients.
